```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, dpi = 110, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This guide covers the first step of the networkflow pipeline: building the
network. It explains what a projected network is, how the similarity
between two documents is measured, and which choices (measure, threshold,
time windows) shape the network before any cluster is detected. The next
guides cover [finding and reading clusters](finding-and-reading-clusters.html)
and [following clusters over time](following-clusters-over-time.html).

## Why networks?

Since the 1970s, the number of articles published in most disciplines has
grown so much that no historian or sociologist of science can read a
whole literature. Citation data offer another entry point: by citing,
authors say which works they build on, and the references that articles
share reveal groups of works addressing similar questions with similar
tools. Mapping these groups, their size and their evolution, has become a
common tool of the history and sociology of science, including the
history of economics [@claveau2016; @edwards2018; @cherrier2018;
@goutsmedt2023quantitative].

networkflow was written for this kind of research. It organises the
analysis as a *pipeline*: building networks from tabular data, detecting
clusters, following them over time, naming and plotting them. Each step is
a function whose choices are explicit arguments, so that they can be
discussed, varied and reported. The functions were developed for, and
used in, studies of European macroeconomics [@goutsmedt2023eer], of the
explanations of the 1970s stagflation [@goutsmedt2021], of the history of
the concept of rationality [@delcey2026] and of the scientific reception
of a report on the environmental impact of livestock [@duluins2026].

## The example data

The examples use the corpus of @goutsmedt2021: the books and articles that
tried to explain the US stagflation of the 1970s, published between 1975
and 2013, and the references they cite.

```{r}
#| label: data
library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
nrow(nodes)
head(Ref_stagflation[, c("source_id", "target_id", "target_author", "target_year")])
```

`Nodes_stagflation` has one row per document, `Ref_stagflation` one row per
citation: document `source_id` cites document `target_id`. This is the
typical shape of research data: not a network, but a table of links
between two kinds of entities.

## From a two-mode relation to a network

### Projection

Citations link two sets of entities: citing documents and cited
references. Such a *two-mode*, or *bipartite*, relation can be written as a
matrix $A$ with one row per citing document, one column per reference, and
$a_{ij} = 1$ when document $i$ cites reference $j$. To study the citing
documents, we *project* this relation onto them: two documents are linked
when they cite the same references. The raw strength of the tie is the
number of shared references,

$$
c_{ik} = \sum_j a_{ij} a_{kj} = |R_i \cap R_k|,
$$

with $R_i$ the bibliography of document $i$. In matrix form, $C = A A^\top$.
This is **bibliographic coupling** [@kessler1963]: two articles are coupled
when their bibliographies overlap. Projecting on the other set gives
**co-citation** [@small1973]: two references are linked when they are
cited together, $A^\top A$. The two networks answer different questions.
Coupling groups the citing documents, and is fixed once they are published:
it maps the *research fronts* of a period. Co-citation groups the cited
works, and evolves as new articles cite them: it maps the *intellectual
base* of a literature as its users see it. Comparing the clusters
obtained on two million biomedical articles, @boyack2010 found that
bibliographic coupling slightly outperformed co-citation in representing
research fronts, direct citation being the least accurate; @yan2012 show how the
various scholarly networks (coupling, co-citation, co-authorship,
co-words) relate to each other.

The same logic applies far beyond citations: authors and the papers they
sign (co-authorship), accounts and the hashtags they use, members and the
boards they sit on. `build_network()` projects any such table, given a
`source_id` (the entities that become nodes) and a `target_id` (the
entities that link them).

```{r}
#| label: build
network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)
network
```

The result is a `tbl_graph` from tidygraph: a node table (the columns of
`nodes`) and an edge table (`from`, `to`, `weight`), which can be
manipulated with dplyr verbs and drawn with ggraph. Documents without any
shared reference are dropped (`keep_singleton = FALSE`).

### Measuring similarity

Raw counts are a poor measure of similarity. An article with 150
references shares some with almost every other article; two short notes
sharing three references may be much closer. Normalised measures correct
for this. With $L_i$ the length of the bibliography of $i$, $N$ the number
of citing documents and $f_j$ the number of documents citing reference $j$,
the three measures available through biblionetwork
[@goutsmedt2023biblionetwork] are:

- the **coupling angle**, the cosine of the two bibliographies
  [@sen1983]:
  $$w_{ik} = \frac{|R_i \cap R_k|}{\sqrt{L_i L_k}};$$
- the **coupling strength** [@vladutz1984; @shen2019], which gives less
  weight to the references that everybody cites, in the spirit of the
  inverse document frequency of text mining:
  $$w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{L_i L_k};$$
- the **coupling similarity**, inspired by @shen2019, which normalises the
  same weighted sum by the weighted length of each bibliography,
  $S_i = \sum_{j \in R_i} \log(N / f_j)$:
  $$w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{S_i S_k}.$$

Sharing a citation of Taylor's 1993 article on policy rules, cited by 22
documents of the corpus, says less about two explanations of the
stagflation than sharing a reference cited by only two: the second and
third measures encode this idea.

All measures assume that a work has a single identifier. Raw citation
strings do not guarantee it: in `Ref_stagflation`, Friedman's 1968 "The Role
of Monetary Policy" is written with six different author strings and two
titles. Here this is harmless, because the data come with a `target_id`
that the database assigned to each cited work: the 20 citations share the
same identifier, and the documents citing it are coupled. Without such an
identifier, each spelling would be a different reference, and two documents
citing the same work in different ways would not share it. Even with
identifiers, matching is never perfect: about 1.5% of the works of
`Ref_stagflation` (28 of 1,856 distinct titles, after removing punctuation
and comparing with the year) are attached to more than one `target_id`. Check the most
cited references for duplicates before building a network, and clean them
when they matter: the [last guide](beyond-bibliographic-coupling.html)
explains why this matters most for co-citation.

How different are the measures in practice? We compute the three networks
and compare the weights of the same pairs.

```{r}
#| label: measures
measures <- c("coupling_angle", "coupling_strength", "coupling_similarity")
weights <- lapply(measures, function(measure) {
  graph <- build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    projection_method = "structured",
    cooccurrence_method = measure,
    edges_threshold = 1
  )
  ids <- tidygraph::as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes")$source_id
  edges <- tidygraph::as_tibble(graph, active = "edges")
  data.frame(
    pair = paste(pmin(ids[edges$from], ids[edges$to]), pmax(ids[edges$from], ids[edges$to])),
    weight = edges$weight
  )
})
pairs <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "pair"), weights)
names(pairs) <- c("pair", measures)
round(cor(pairs[, measures], method = "spearman"), 3)
```

The three measures keep the same pairs (the threshold applies to the raw
count) but weight them differently. Coupling strength and coupling
similarity rank the pairs identically, and not by chance: in the current
version of biblionetwork, the normalisation $S_i$ of the coupling
similarity gives every reference the weight of the first one, so that
$S_i$ is proportional to $L_i$ and the measure is proportional to the
coupling strength. Until this is corrected, coupling strength and coupling
angle are the two distinct options. The coupling angle, which treats all
references alike, departs more from the coupling strength. A rank
correlation of 0.84 still leaves room for different clusters at the
margin: when the conclusions of a study rest on the exact composition of a
cluster, it is worth checking them with a second measure.

### Thresholds

Most pairs of articles in a literature share one or two classic
references. These ties say little, and they make the network dense
(`edges_threshold = 1` links a quarter of all pairs here). Raising the
threshold keeps the pairs that share at least $n$ references:

```{r}
#| label: thresholds
thresholds <- data.frame(threshold = 1:4)
thresholds[c("nodes", "edges", "components")] <- t(sapply(thresholds$threshold, function(n) {
  graph <- build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    projection_method = "structured",
    cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
    edges_threshold = n
  )
  c(igraph::vcount(graph), igraph::ecount(graph), igraph::components(graph)$no)
}))
thresholds
```

Each step removes many edges, but also documents, which no longer share
enough references with any other, and breaks the network into components.
There is no right threshold: it depends on the length of bibliographies
and on the size of the corpus. A threshold of 2 is a common choice for
article corpora; in a corpus of short documents with few references, 1
may be the only option.

### A statistical alternative: backbones

A threshold is the same for every pair. Yet sharing two references means
little for two articles with 150 references each, and a lot for two notes
with five. The *backbone* approach replaces the fixed threshold with a
test [@neal2014]: for each pair, is the number of shared targets larger
than in random bipartite networks that keep some properties of the
observed one? The stochastic degree sequence model (`model = "sdsm"`)
keeps, on average, the number of references of each document and the
number of citations of each reference; the backbone package
[@domagalski2021; @neal2022] computes the probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: backbone
backbone <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "statistical",
  model = "sdsm",
  alpha = 0.05
)
c(nodes = igraph::vcount(backbone), edges = igraph::ecount(backbone))
```

The backbone keeps the ties that are unlikely under the null model at the
5% level. Its edges are unweighted: each edge means "more shared
references than expected", whatever the number. The approach is slower on
large corpora, and with many pairs tested, multiple-test corrections
(`backbone_args = list(mtc = "holm")`) remove many more edges. It is a
useful check of a threshold-based network, and the better option when the
lengths of the target lists vary a lot.

### Components

Projected networks often have one large component and small islands.
Community detection and layouts are hard to read on islands, and
`filter_components()` keeps the largest component(s), with a warning if a
large one is dropped:

```{r}
#| label: components
network_2 <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 2
)
main_component <- filter_components(network_2)
c(before = igraph::vcount(network_2), after = igraph::vcount(main_component))
```

Before dropping documents, look at them: a small component may be a
marginal literature that matters to the story.

## Time windows

A network of the whole period mixes literatures that did not coexist.
`build_dynamic_networks()` builds one network per time window: a window
starting in year $s$ gathers the documents published in
$[s, s + w - 1]$, $w$ being `time_window`, and the network is computed as
if the corpus were limited to them. Windows can be successive
(`overlapping_window = FALSE`: 1975-1984, 1985-1994...) or sliding
(`TRUE`: 1975-1984, 1976-1985...).

```{r}
#| label: dynamic
networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 10,
  overlapping_window = TRUE,
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  filter_components = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
length(networks)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-window-size
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Number of documents in the main component of each ten-year window, from
#|   1975-1984 to 2004-2013: high in the first windows, very low for windows
#|   centred on the late 1980s, and rising again from the mid-1990s.
window_sizes <- data.frame(
  window = names(networks),
  start = as.integer(substr(names(networks), 1, 4)),
  nodes = sapply(networks, igraph::vcount)
)
ggplot(window_sizes, aes(start, nodes)) +
  geom_col(fill = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = window_sizes$start[seq(1, nrow(window_sizes), by = 5)],
    labels = window_sizes$window[seq(1, nrow(window_sizes), by = 5)],
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Window", y = "Documents in the main component") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

The size of the windows tells a story of its own: the stagflation was
widely debated in the late 1970s and early 1980s, interest faded after the
mid-1980s, and a new literature on it emerged in the 1990s, the pattern
that @goutsmedt2021 describes. It also
warns about a technical limit: windows centred on the late 1980s contain
about ten documents, too few for their clusters to mean much. The choice
of the window is substantive. It should be long enough for each network
to have enough documents to show a structure, and short enough for
changes to be visible. Sliding windows smooth the evolution (consecutive
networks share 90% of their period here) and make clusters easier to
follow; successive windows give independent snapshots.

## What comes next

The networks are ready for [community detection](finding-and-reading-clusters.html).
Each choice made here (measure, threshold, window) changes them: report
these choices, and check that the main results hold under reasonable
alternatives.
